newsitem.title: USA: Kim Phuc, recalled in Vietnam photo, lays wreath.
newsitem.headline: Kim Phuc, recalled in Vietnam photo, lays wreath.

text.p: Phan Thi Kim Phuc, a Vietnamese villager whose pain and terror during a 1972 napalm attack were captured in a prize-winning photograph, on Monday laid a wreath of remembrance at the Vietnam Veterans Memorial.
In halting English, Kim told a graying audience of thousands on Veterans Day:

"As you know, I am the little girl who was running to escape from the napalm fire. I do not want to talk about the war. I cannot change history. I only want you to remember the tragedy of war in order to do things to stop fighting and killing around the world."

Kim was the central figure in a news photograph that galvanised U.S. anti-war sentiment. The picture showed Kim, then 9, running naked and screaming down a road in her village of Trang Bang outside Saigon.

She had torn off her burning clothes after being hit by napalm dropped by South Vietnamese forces on a temple where she and her family took refuge. She lost consciousness moments after the famous photograph was taken, and the photographer, Nick Ut, took her to a hospital.
The photograph, which at first was not distributed because of fears newspaper editors would object to the child's nudity, was ultimately seen around the world and won a Pulitzer Prize.

"Even if I could talk face-to-face with the pilot who dropped the bombs, I could tell him we cannot change history but we should try to do good things for the present and for the future to promote peace," Kim said.

She laid a wreath of flowers at the memorial accompanied by retired U.S. Air Force Col. Norm McDaniel, who spent six years as a prisoner of war. Kim got a standing ovation when she began speaking and again when she finished, but her presence was not universally welcomed.

"I'm a little confused about why she's here; she didn't need to be," said Mike Robinson, who stood with the National 4th Infantry Division Association. "Do you know how many civilians were killed in war? They didn't blame anybody, it was their war and she's blaming some pilot. I think it's very inappropriate."

But another with the 4th Infantry association, Roger Barton, acted on a last-minute impulse to give Kim a flower left over from the group's boutonnieres. "I thought she was more deserving," Barton said.
Kim, now 32, took a tortuous road to sit on a makeshift stage in front of the black granite of the Vietnam Veterans Memorial, which is inscribed with the names of more than 58,000 U.S. war dead.

Horribly burned by napalm, she served a propaganda function in Vietnam after the war ended. Eventually she was sent to study and receive medical treatment in Cuba, where she met her husband. After a honeymoon in Moscow, the two defected when the returning flight stopped in Newfoundland. They currently live in Toronto with their son.
